newsitem.title: ITALY: Tug-of-war over lira entry into ERM to go on.
newsitem.headline: Tug-of-war over lira entry into ERM to go on.

text.p: Italy is on course to return to the European Union's currency grid before the end of the year but a tug-of-war with France -- stung by cheap Italian imports -- over what rate the lira gets back in is far from over.
"What is very clear is that the lira will go in and that it will enter in 1996 and not in 1997," saod David Brown, Chief European economist for Bear Stearns in London.
Italian Treasury minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said in Luxembourg on Tuesday he wanted the lira back in the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) by the end of the year.

The lira's present market level -- it was trading at around 993 against the mark on Tuesday -- should be a starting point for talks with Italy's European partners on a new central parity level for the lira, said Ciampi.
Most economists see the lira going back into the ERM at between 950 and 1,000 lire to the mark.

But France's Finance Minister, Jean Arthuis, firing the latest shot in a war of words aimed at encouraging a strengthening of the lira, has said the Italian currency should not be bundled back into the grid in a hurry.
"To be hasty on the re-entry (of the lira) would mean to take a risk ... which would cause harm to the Italian and European authorities," said Arthuis.
Italy sees an early lira return to the ERM as a way of showing its determination to qualify for an advance party of countries joining a European economic and monetary union (EMU) by 1999.
The Maastricht treaty laying down guidelines for joining EMU, says aspiring members should enjoy two years of currency stability within the ERM before applying to join the single currency club.
Italy intends to make its return to the ERM as soon as a 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) budget package for 1997 has cleared the main hurdles in parliament. The budget must be approved by year-end.

The French, who have consistently pursued a strong currency policy in recent years, see the return of the lira to the ERM as a chance to blunt the competitive edge Italy gained after its currency's ignominious exit from the currency grid in 1992.
"The French don't want the lira tied back in with a strong competitive advantage in exports. They are very worried about cheap Italian imports," said Brown.

The lira depreciated by about 40 percent against the French franc after its 1992 ejection from the ERM and has since recovered about half its value but French officials say it still has more "catching up" to do.
French President Jacques Chirac has taken up the cause of French businessmen in blaming a cheap lira for unleashing a flood of cheap car and textiles imports.
While the French are leaning heavily on the Italians to let their currency rise in value, Italy's industrialists are clamouring for the exact oppositite to happen.

Giorgio Fossa, the president of the Italian employers' association, Confindustria, warned last week that the lira had risen too steeply in recent weeks and appealed for caution at a time when the economy is hovering close to recession.
The frictions were thrown into stark relief earlier this month when Jacques Calvet, chairman of French auto group PSA Peugeot Citroen said the lira had to gain in strength.
The head of rival Italian group Fiat 's cars division, Roberto Testore, hit back by saying the lira was overvalued and calling for an exchange rate of 1,040 against the mark.

Underlying French and Italian anxieties over their respective exchange rates are fears that an economic slowdown will scupper attempts to meet a key Maastricht target -- a ratio of public debt to gross domestic product of three percent.
Few economists believe Italy can meet this goal by the end of 1997 but France is still in with a chance.
